title: Quantum annealers as programmable thermal machines
authors: Jakub Pawłowski, Tomasz Śmierzchalski, Fengping Jin, Bartłomiej Gardas, Sebastian Deffner, Zakaria Mzaouali
abstract: Programmable quantum annealers are used for optimization, probabilistic sampling, and simulation, but their performance is commonly reported without the energy exchanged during computation. Here we characterize the D-Wave quantum annealer as a closed thermodynamic cycle. From initial and final Ising energies and an effective temperature fitted to the output distribution, we obtain lower bounds on entropy production, environment energy exchange, work, and power. By varying the prepared distribution and the reverse annealing turning point, we map heater-, accelerator-, refrigerator-, and engine-compatible regimes in one dimensional chains and higher connectivity instances, and apply the same analysis to Advantage and Advantage2 hardware. For an encoded optimization problem, the measured processor energy change states whether final candidates improve or worsen the programmed objective on average. For sampling, the fitted temperature provides an operational measure of how strongly probability is concentrated among low energy configurations. The thermodynamic mode therefore adds information absent from solution quality or runtime alone: it distinguishes driven refinement, net heating, and heat pumping while quantifying their energetic consequences. This framework connects quantum optimization, probabilistic computing, statistical physics simulation, hardware diagnostics, and energy-aware assessment without assuming that a thermodynamic label alone determines computational performance.
summary: The paper develops a thermodynamic framework to analyze quantum annealers by treating them as closed thermal cycles. It uses fluctuation theorems to calculate energy exchange quantities like work and entropy production from measured energy changes. This allows researchers to diagnose the underlying physical process—whether it is net heating, cooling, or controlled work extraction—providing deeper insight than performance metrics alone.
main_problem: The paper aims to characterize programmable quantum annealers as closed thermodynamic cycles to assess performance beyond simple solution quality or runtime metrics.
main_result: By applying fluctuation theorems, the authors derive lower bounds on entropy production, work, and heat exchange, revealing operational regimes (heater, refrigerator, etc.) that quantify energy flow during computation.
method: The methodology involves treating the annealer as a thermodynamic system undergoing reverse annealing cycles, using initial/final Ising energies and effective temperature fits to calculate these thermodynamic bounds.
model_or_system: The primary physical platform is the D-Wave quantum annealer (and Advantage hardware), modeled via an Ising Hamiltonian. The analysis applies to 1D chains and higher connectivity instances.
key_observables: Lower bounds on entropy production ($\Sigma$), Work ($W$), Heat ($Q$), Power ($P$), and the effective environment temperature ($T_2$).
important_parameters: Initial inverse temperature ($ eta_1$), annealing parameter ($s_p$), cycle time ($	au$), and system size ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fluctuation identities (like TURs) to derive bounds from limited measurements, and the extracted $T_2$ is an effective temperature of sampled degrees of freedom, not a direct hardware measurement.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental workflow using reverse annealing cycles; one shows finite size scaling of work/power bounds for 1D chains, another maps operating modes in the $( eta_1, s_p)$ plane, and others show thermodynamic scans varying initial temperature.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the thermodynamic framework by defining the cycle, applies this to measure energy exchange on D-Wave hardware across different annealing paths, classifies the operational regime based on input parameters ($ eta_1, s_p$), and concludes with device-agnostic diagnostic tools.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous connection between quantum computation performance metrics (like optimization success) and fundamental principles of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, offering new diagnostics for open quantum systems.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Experimental workflow of the paper. A classical Gibbs state of the programmed Ising Hamil- tonian is prepared at unitless inverse temperature β1 = 1 and used as the input state for a reverse annealing schedule. The annealing parameter is ramped from s = 1 to a turning point sp and back to s = 1, so that the initial and final Hamiltonians are the same. The quantum processing unit readout therefore gives a two point energy change ∆E1 of the problem Hamiltonian. Repeating the cycle builds the distribution of ∆E1, from which we estimate an effective environment temperature T2 by pseudo-likelihood thermometry and evaluate fluctuation relation and thermodynamic uncertainty relation bounds...

Fig. 2: Finite size scaling of thermodynamic bounds in a one dimensional chain. For random uniform chains with strong random fields, hi ∈[−2, 2], the reverse annealing turning point is fixed at sp = 0.35 and the chain length L is varied on the D-Wave Advantage6.4 (Pegasus) chip. Panel (a) shows the pseudo-likelihood estimate of the effective temperature T2 for annealing times τ = 100, 500, 1000 and 2000 µs. Panels (b) and (c) show the work and power bounds per spin, which grow slowly with L and are consistent with a logarithmic finite size enhancement over the range studied. Panel (d) shows the total power bound, which grows approximately as L log L when the per-spin contribution is summed...

Fig. 7: Burn-in diagnostics for the Gibbs initial samples. Sample energy E and magnetization M are shown as functions of the number of burn-in sweeps for the RAU (upper row) and CBFM (lower row) Pegasus P6 instances. In both cases the energy reaches a plateau after an initial relaxation period. The RAU magnetization fluctuates around zero, while the CBFM magnetization remains finite because of the biased ferromagnetic structure of the instance. The plateau region is used to choose the burn-in length for the production samples.
